narrative:
The model estimated an 85.9% probability that you would fail the bar exam on your first attempt. That is a high predicted risk, and it is why your law-school application was denied: the admissions decision treated the likely bar outcome as too uncertain to justify admission as submitted. This is a prediction, not a certainty, but it means the application would need stronger evidence of bar readiness.

The most influential factor was your third-year class standing. You were in the lowest decile, while accepted students averaged around the sixth decile; this strongly pushed the prediction toward bar failure. The second most important factor was your law-school admission test score of 22, well below the accepted-student average of about 37, which also pushed toward failure. The third factor was your first-year class standing: again being in the lowest decile, compared with an accepted average near the sixth decile, added further risk. All three top factors pointed in the same direction—toward likely failure—rather than offsetting one another.

To improve your chances if you reapply, focus first on raising your admission test score through structured preparation and a retake if feasible. Seek academic advising about your class performance and whether additional coursework, a post-baccalaureate record, or an explanatory statement can demonstrate improvement. Ask admissions for feedback, and connect with bar-prep resources early so you can present a concrete readiness plan.
